ground_truth.description: Cross-denominated bonus calculation assumes thresholdCross >= balanceCross, but distribution insolvency (one token below requirement while another has surplus) causes balanceCross > thresholdCross. Unsigned arithmetic underflows and reverts.
ground_truth.root_cause: Cross-denominated bonus calculation assumes thresholdCross >= balanceCross, but distribution insolvency (one token below requirement while another has surplus) causes balanceCross > thresholdCross. Unsigned arithmetic underflows and reverts.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: High utilization disables cross-margining. User holds large token0 surplus but token1 deficit. Liquidation call reverts on bonus calculation.
ground_truth.fix_description: Clamp the deficit: uint256 deficitCross = thresholdCross > balanceCross ? thresholdCross - balanceCross : 0;

vulnerabilities.type: Missing access control / re-initialization leading to wallet takeover
vulnerabilities.explanation: BuilderWallet.init(address _builderAdmin) is an external function with no access control and no one-time initialization guard. Any address can call init at any time and overwrite builderAdmin. BuilderAdmin is the sole authority allowed to call sweep(), which transfers the wallet’s entire ERC20 balance to an arbitrary recipient. Since these BuilderWallets are used as deterministic fee recipients (via RiskEngine _computeBuilderWallet), an attacker can seize control of any deployed BuilderWallet and steal all fee tokens held there, without compromising the protocol owner/guardian.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1) Identify a deployed BuilderWallet address (e.g., from BuilderFactory events, or by computing it via the CREATE2 formula / observing fee recipient addresses used by the protocol).
2) Call BuilderWallet.init(attackerAddress) from any EOA; this overwrites builderAdmin.
3) Call BuilderWallet.sweep(token, attackerEOA) for each token held in the wallet.
4) All balances in those tokens are transferred to the attacker.
This works even if the factory already initialized the wallet correctly, because init can be called again to reassign admin.

prediction.overall_explanation: The main RiskEngine logic shown is largely view/pure math and does not itself expose obvious permissionless fund-moving paths. However, the auxiliary BuilderWallet used as a deterministic fee recipient is critically vulnerable: its init() function is publicly callable and can be re-called to overwrite builderAdmin, allowing any attacker to take control and sweep all ERC20 tokens from any deployed BuilderWallet. This is a direct, permissionless theft vector for protocol/builder fee flows.
